what_its_for: Letrozole is used to treat certain types of breast cancer in women who have gone through menopause. It works by lowering the amount of estrogen in your body, which helps slow or stop the growth of some breast tumors that need estrogen to grow. It may also be used to help prevent breast cancer from coming back.
how_to_take: Take letrozole by mouth, with or without food. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. Try to take it at the same time every day to help you remember. Do not crush, chew, or break the tablet unless your doctor tells you to.
dosing: The usual dose is one 2.5 mg tablet taken once a day. Always take the dose your doctor prescribed. Do not take more or less than directed. Your doctor will decide how long you need to take this medicine, which may be for several years.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose and remember it on the same day, take it as soon as you remember. If it is already the next day, skip the missed dose and take your next scheduled dose as usual. Do not take two doses on the same day to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store letrozole at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep this medicine out of the reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about the best way to dispose of it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid becoming pregnant while taking letrozole, as it can seriously harm an unborn baby. Use reliable birth control if there is any chance you could become pregnant, even if you think you are in menopause. Avoid taking estrogen-containing medicines (such as hormone replacement therapy) while on letrozole, as they may reduce how well it works. Limit alcohol, as it can increase the risk of bone loss. Talk to your doctor before taking any new medicines, vitamins, or herbal supplements.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you experience: chest pain or shortness of breath (possible blood clot), severe bone, joint, or muscle pain, signs of liver problems such as yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, or severe stomach pain, signs of high cholesterol such as chest pain or trouble breathing, unusual vaginal bleeding, swelling in your hands, feet, or legs, memory problems or confusion, or signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, hives, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing.
when_it_works: Letrozole starts lowering estrogen levels in your body fairly quickly, but you may not notice changes in your condition right away. It may take several weeks to months before your doctor can tell how well it is working. It is important to keep taking it every day even if you feel fine, because it is working in the background to help control your cancer.
special_populations: Older adults (65 and over): Letrozole can be used safely in older women, but bone loss (osteoporosis) may be a greater concern. Your doctor may recommend calcium, vitamin D, or bone-strengthening medicines. Liver problems: If you have severe liver disease, your dose may need to be adjusted. Tell your doctor about any liver conditions. Kidney problems: Letrozole is generally safe for people with kidney problems at the usual dose, but always inform your doctor. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Letrozole must NOT be used during pregnancy as it can cause serious birth defects or loss of the baby. It should also not be used while breastfeeding. Women who are not yet in menopause: If you are still having periods or recently entered menopause, talk to your doctor, as special precautions may apply.
